direct_claims: This dataset is about survival ages across different parts of the population in multiple countries.
The title is "Survival ages across the population."

The expert note says each value represents the number of years that a specific share of the population would survive if people born in that year experienced that year's age-specific death rates throughout life.

The table compares countries including Denmark, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Sweden, Austria, Belgium, Canada, France, Hong Kong, Iceland, Japan, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, South Korea, Spain, Switzerland, Taiwan, the United States, England and Wales, Ireland, and Italy.
The source link provided is an Our World in Data grapher URL.
The data are organized by percentile-like survival cutoffs from 99% through 10% plus a "Top 1%" column.
These values are period-based survival ages rather than literal predictions for one real birth cohort's eventual lifespan.
They summarize what would happen under the mortality conditions observed in the named year if those conditions stayed constant across the life course.
The dataset mixes years across countries, with some entries from 2024, many from 2023, and some from 2022, so comparisons are not perfectly same-year.
The provided table is incomplete because it explicitly notes that 5 more rows are truncated.

Among the listed 2023 entries, Hong Kong has the highest Top 1% survival age at 105.3 years. — derived by scanning Top 1% values for 2023 rows.
Among the listed rows, the United States has the lowest 99% survival age at 22.5 years. — derived by scanning the 99% column across provided rows.

This larger gap suggests more spread between typical and exceptionally long survival in the United States than in Denmark among the listed rows. — derived by comparing the two computed gaps.

The difference between countries is substantial in the provided rows: at the 50% survival point, Hong Kong is at 87.39 years while Latvia is at 79.44 years, a gap of 7.95 years. — derived by subtraction.
At the Top 1% survival point, Hong Kong reaches 105.3 years while Latvia is at 99.9 years, a gap of 5.4 years. — derived by subtraction.

These gaps imply that mortality conditions differ enough across countries to shift not just average survival but also the ages reached by the longest-lived people. — derived from cross-country differences across multiple percentile columns.
